Email is an art form

Every channel you own has its own rules. Video is an art form. A LinkedIn post is an art form. Email is one too — and it builds the closest relationship, because it's the only place you write to one person.

Video

You're performing.

The craft is attention
Social · webinars · blogs

You're broadcasting.

The craft is interruption
Email

You're confiding.

The craft is trust

You'd never expect to be good at video without learning how video works. Email is the same. It's a skill, not a personality trait.

No. Absolutely not.
It never has been, and it never will be.

So why does it feel dead?

playing with it

Instagram ships a new format every year

  • Stories
  • Reels

Email got none of that for twenty years. So it started to feel like a fax machine.

That's changing, right now

  • Images and animated GIFs rendering properly
  • Your logo showing in the inbox

The craft is being reinvented while almost nobody is watching.

And why you can't leave this another year

The smartest operators
have already moved

Steven Bartlett. Jay Shetty. Tony Robbins. Alex Hormozi. Every one of them launched a newsletter in 2025 — while sitting on some of the largest social followings on earth.

They didn't do it for reach. They did it because they know that owned channel is supremacy. A following you rent is not an asset.

We are not building you a newsletter so you can sell.
We are building it so you can create trust.

Everything else — the enquiries, the contracts, the referrals — is what trust does on its own. And the sooner you claim your audience, the cheaper it is to claim.

Act I · The stack

There are 14 kinds of email.
Most businesses send 2.

01Paradigm shiftChanges how they see the problem"You don't have a discipline problem. You have an environment problem."
02ConceptA new idea, research, a mindset shift"A study on why 6 minutes of breathwork beats an hour of trying to relax"
03Problem–solutionNames the problem, shows your fix"Can't switch off at night? Start with the 6-Phase Meditation."
04StorytellingA narrative carries the point"I'm turning 50. So I decided to live 100 lives."
05Social proofSomeone else's result sells for you"Sandra changed one habit at 58. Here's which one."
06CredibilityYour authority. Forbes, 20 years, 400 jobs"Meet the teacher: 20 years, three bestsellers, one method"
07PersuasionPure sales, built as an argument"Three reasons to start your Quest before Sunday"
08Direct promoThe offer. Discount, Black Friday, New Year"Black Friday: every Quest, one price"
09Last callThe deadline. Scarcity, used honestly"Doors close tonight at midnight"
10AnnouncementThis new thing exists"Introducing Vishen's new Quest"
11InvitationCome to this. Your RSVP is on hold"You're invited: AI Summit 2026. Free, 20–22 March."
12WWWWWhat, when, why, who. The logistics email"AI Summit: what, when, why, and who's speaking"
13Video emailOne image, one link, almost no text"Watch: Vishen on the AI-First Method, 12 minutes"
14ListicleThree, five or seven things"5 morning habits from our longevity teachers"

Illustrative examples in Mindvalley's voice — the same fourteen jobs work in yours.

Act I · The zoom-in

Then there's the newsletter.

Every one of those fourteen spends trust. The newsletter is the only thing you send that deposits it.

Your promo email doesn't fail because of the copy. It fails because it was the first time that person had heard from you in four months.

So the rule for the rest of your business life: the newsletter runs always. Campaigns sit on top of it, three or four times a year. Never the other way round.

Act I · A tour of what already exists

Five models. Every good newsletter
in the world is one of these.

01 · The Curator

You read the firehose so they don't have to. Filtered, plain English, same slots every time.

Real example: Morning Brew — daily business news, no jargon, actually funny
For: anyone in a fast-moving or regulated trade
02 · The Teacher

One idea, explained properly. No news, no urgency, identical shape every issue.

Real example: James Clear's 3-2-1 — every Thursday: 3 ideas, 2 quotes, 1 question
For: coaches, consultants, advisors
03 · The Practitioner's Log

One thing you actually did in your business this week, and what happened when you did it.

Real example: Justin Welsh, The Saturday Solopreneur — one tactic from his own work, 3-minute read
For: most people in this room
04 · The Deep Dive

One properly researched piece a week. Interviews, data, frameworks. Long.

Real example: Lenny's Newsletter — 1,000+ words, 10–20 hours per issue, people pay for it
For: anyone who genuinely loves writing
05 · The Trade Brief

Narrow niche, high value, deliberately unglamorous. Written for one job title.

Real example: Stratechery — one analyst, one professional audience, thousands of paying subscribers
For: services where your buyer is a job title
The thing to notice

Four of the five don't require you to be a writer. They're you reporting on things that already happen.

Only the Deep Dive needs you to love writing. Don't pick it because it looks impressive.
Act I · Not prescribed — worked out

So which one is yours?
Let's do it out loud.

I'm not going to tell you. I'm going to ask four questions and you'll hear the answer land.

  1. Who's the one person you want reading it? Not a market — one actual client you've had.
  2. What do they say in the first ten minutes of a call, before you've fixed anything?
  3. What do you know that most of them find genuinely surprising?
  4. Could you write one of these on your worst week of the month?

Answer those four and your model picks itself.

1

Know yourself

Because you can't write what you haven't decided
Gear 1 · The Mirror

Founders don't have writer's block.
They have position block.

Nobody here struggles to talk for an hour about their business. Put the same person in front of a blank email and nothing comes out.

Talking lets you hedge. Writing makes you commit. That's the whole difference.

Your Personal Brand OS captured how you sound. It never asked what you think. And voice without a position is a very well-dressed person with nothing to say.

The seven Mirror questions

Answer these once, properly, and you'll never be short of something to say. Prompt 1 at the end of this deck walks you through them, one at a time.

Gear 1 · Pillars

Four themes. Two years.

The subjects you commit to being known for. Everything you publish sits inside one of them.

  • Four, not six. More than five and you'll forget which one you're writing for.
  • A pillar is a theme, not a topic. "How we price jobs" is a pillar. "Tuesday's issue" isn't.
  • The competitor test: would another business in your space use these exact four? Narrow them until they wouldn't.
  • Never two issues from the same pillar back to back. That one rule solves drift and repetition forever.
A plumbing contractor
  • Pricing and quoting honestly — authority
  • What goes wrong on site, and why — authority
  • Compliance and regulation changes — authority
  • Running a crew — affinity
A high-ticket coach
  • Where founder energy actually goes — authority
  • The decisions that burn people out — authority
  • What I get wrong in my own week — affinity
  • What clients say in the first ten minutes — authority

Gear 2 · Two sources you're throwing away

Your camera roll, and every event you go to

Casual photos

  • The job — before, during, the ugly middle
  • The thing that broke, and the part that caused it
  • A whiteboard, a van, the site at 7am

Badly lit and real beats staged. Never stock photography — it reads as a lie. The caption is the content.

One event = three issues

  • Before — the one thing I want to find out
  • After — what changes what I do on Monday
  • Later — what everyone there believed that I think is wrong

Nobody cares that you went. They care what it means for them.

Make it land

Being read is a craft, not a mood
Gear 3 · The story shape

The Seven Beats of your newsletter

01
The feeling
Something they already feel, before you name anything. No throat-clearing.
02
The scene
One moment. A time, a place, a person, a number.
03
The turn
The thing that surprised you.
04
The name
Now name the idea — a label they can repeat to a colleague.
05
The proof
A number or a second example. In a sentence, never a bullet dump.
06
The transfer
What they do about it. One to three things, doable tomorrow.
07
The ask
One. Never two.

Lead with the lesson and bolt an example on afterwards and it reads as a lecture. Put them in the moment first, and let them arrive at the point with you.

Gear 3 · What good actually looks like

Three openings that work

A trade

A Tuesday in February. A quote for £4,200 I was certain I'd lost.

The client rang to say the other lot came in at £2,500. So I said: "Theirs doesn't include making good. You'll pay for the plaster either way — the only question is whether you pay it now or in March."

She went with us.

Scene · turn · the exact sentence · outcome
A coach

A client told me last week she'd been "productive all day and couldn't name one thing she'd done."

I've heard that sentence maybe forty times this year.

It isn't a time problem. Nothing she did that day had a finish line.

Their words · frequency as proof · the reframe
A service business

We lost a contract last month because of a bin.

Not the cleaning. A bin left in the wrong corridor on a Friday, three weeks running.

Nobody complained. They just didn't renew.

Specific · surprising · the lesson does itself

All three: a real moment, a real number or a real sentence someone said — and no moral tacked on the end.

Gear 3 · Keeping it honest

Four rules

Do

  • One story per issue. Three is a magazine, and nobody finishes a magazine.
  • Specific beats big. "A Tuesday in February, £4,200" beats "life-changing results".
  • Be the one who got it wrong first. Not the hero.
  • Say the moral once, or not at all.

Never

  • Rags-to-riches claims. "Broke to six figures in 90 days" reads as a scam even when it's true.
  • Invent or composite a client. One made-up detail contaminates everything you'll ever write.
  • Use a client's name without asking. "A client asked me last week" is always enough.

Gear 3 · Format 3

The listicle — your most
forwarded format

  • The number goes in the subject line. Odd numbers: 3, 5, 7.
  • One line of framing, then straight into item one. No introduction.
  • Each item: a bold label, two or three sentences, one specific detail.
  • No item longer than four lines. If one runs long, it was its own issue.
  • Best item last. People remember last and forward last.

Why it earns its place: it's the most skimmable format in email, and the easiest to forward — someone can send it on with "see number 4". 300–600 words.

Examples: "3 things I get asked on every site visit." · "5 questions to ask before signing a maintenance contract."

Before you go looking for a template

Design does less than you think —
until it does everything

What actually helps

  • One column. Left-aligned. Real text. Plain beats designed, every time.
  • One photo, doing a job. Yours, badly lit, real.
  • Generous line spacing and short paragraphs. That is the design.
  • One button, in your accent colour — the only colour in the whole email.
  • Your logo small, at the bottom. Not a banner at the top.

What hurts

  • A big header image. It pushes your first line below the fold and slows the load.
  • Multi-column layouts. They collapse into nonsense on a phone.
  • Stock photography. Instant loss of trust.
  • Grey text on white. Use near-black. People are reading in daylight.
  • Anything that looks like a brochure. The moment it looks designed, it reads as an advert.

The test: does it look like an email a person sent you, or a campaign a company sent 40,000 people? We design for the first one.

Gear 3 · Voice

How to sound like yourself

Six moves

  • Write to one person. Picture an actual client, use their name in your head.
  • Read it out loud. Anything you stumble on, cut. That's the whole edit.
  • Sentences under 20 words. Paragraphs of one to three.
  • Brackets for warmth. (The closest thing writing has to a smile.)
  • Bold the line you'd say louder. Never a whole paragraph.
  • Keep one weird thing. Your odd phrase, your sign-off. That's what they remember.

Delete on sight

  • unlock · elevate · journey · game-changer · leverage · seamless · robust · delve
  • "I hope this email finds you well"
  • "In today's fast-paced world"
  • "We're excited to announce"
  • Any sentence that could sit in a competitor's newsletter unchanged

The AI tell: three adjectives in a row and no number. Fix: delete two adjectives, add one number.

Gear 3 · The one thing you never delegate

Humour is the fastest way
to sound human

Which is exactly why Claude can't do it for you. It writes a joke the way it thinks a joke is shaped. It lands one time in twenty — and the other nineteen tell your reader a machine wrote this.

Pick your register — and stay in it
  • Dry — "The quote was accepted. Nobody was more surprised than me."
  • Self-deprecating — "I have now done this wrong in three countries."
  • Deadpan understatement — "It was a fairly memorable Friday."
  • Sarcastic — works, but sparingly, and never about a client.
Yours is one of these. Pick it, and use the same one every issue — that's part of the ritual.
So use the house convention

…and the quote came back at £4,200, more than I'd hoped.

[HUMAN: your dry aside about the client's face here]

But here's what I hadn't expected —

Claude leaves the marker. You fill it in. Eleven seconds, and it's the difference between sounding like you and sounding like everyone.
Gear 3 · Formatting

The first line has one job:
make them read the second

Never

"Hi there! I hope this email finds you well. In today's fast-paced business environment, pricing is one of the most challenging aspects of running a successful contracting business, and many owners struggle to communicate their value effectively…"

Greeting, then context, then throat-clearing. They're gone by word nine.
Instead

"A Tuesday in February. A quote for £4,200 I was certain I'd lost."

"Then the client rang."

No greeting. No context. Start in the middle of the moment.
  • One idea per paragraph, then a line break. On a phone, five lines looks like homework.
  • Bold the four or five phrases that carry the argument — because that's all a skimmer reads.
  • One image, doing a job. A real photo or one clean number. Decoration costs you credibility.
  • Send a test to yourself and read it on your phone. Catches something one time in three.
Gear 3 · Earning the open

Four things decide whether
you get read at all

1 · The from-name

A person, never a company. People open people. Matters more than your subject line.

2 · The subject line

Under 55 characters. Specific, not mysterious.

3 · The preheader

The grey line next to the subject. A free second sentence. Add, never echo.

4 · The first line

Never spend it on "hope you're well".

Get all four right and a small list will out-open a big brand's list every time.

Gear 3 · The thing nobody says

Specific beats mysterious.
Every time.

Your reader isn't deciding whether to be curious. They're deciding, in a fifth of a second, whether you are worth ninety seconds of their morning.

Specificity is the only evidence they have. A number, a price, a date, a confession — that's proof there's something real inside. Mystery is a promise with no collateral, and their inbox is already full of promises.

Tell them exactly what's inside. The ones who want it open every time — and those are the only people who were ever going to buy from you.

The rules

Under 55 characters. No colons. No emojis. Sentence case. Nothing you wouldn't say in a pub. And honest — it must describe what's inside.

4

Make it run

Consistency is the only real moat
Gear 4 · The ask

One ask. Every time.

  • One primary ask per issue. Two means they have to choose, so they do neither.
  • Ask for the next rung. Read → reply → click → book → buy. Skip a rung and you halve the number who move.
  • Write what happens next, not what to do. "See the checklist I use" beats "Click here".
  • 90% useful, 10% selling — across the month, not per email.
  • The reply is the most undervalued ask in business. It costs nothing and it starts a conversation a click never will.
Gear 4 · The gift

Every issue contains something
they could use if they never buy

A specific tip

One thing they can do tomorrow. Free and instant.

A checklist

The list you already run through in your head, written down.

A prompt guide

The five prompts you actually use. The highest-value giveaway of 2026 — and you all already have some.

A template

Your quote wording, your onboarding email.

A quiz or a poll

One click inside the email. It tells you what to write next week.

Something list-only

An early look, a seat, a discount. Never posted publicly. This is what makes them stay.

The test before every send: if they delete this in ten seconds, did they still get something?

Gear 4 · Growth

Put it on the LinkedIn profile
you rebuilt in Week 2

Mock-up · the shape, not a real profile
✉
The Site Notes — every ThursdayOne thing that goes wrong on commercial jobs, and how to stop it. Free.

In your About: "I write The Site Notes every Thursday — one thing that goes wrong on commercial jobs and how to avoid it. Link below."

At the end of a post: "I write about this every Thursday for around 300 property managers. Link in my featured section."

And the rest of it
  • Ask. Out loud. Repeatedly. Most small lists are small because nobody was told it exists.
  • Announce after you send, not just before. After wins — nobody wants to miss the next one.
  • Name the thing they get, don't describe the newsletter. "Get the 5 prompts I use to quote a job in 10 minutes."
  • Your email signature. Free, forever.
  • Ask clients one at a time. Highest conversion of anything here.
Gear 4 · The highest-leverage email you'll ever write

The welcome email

It gets the highest open rate of anything you send — often two to three times a normal issue — because they chose you seconds ago. Almost everyone wastes it.

  • Instantly. Under 150 words. From you, signed by you, replies switched on.
  • Four jobs: confirm what they get and when · deliver the gift immediately · ask one real question · tell them to add you to their contacts.
  • Ask something you actually want answered. Their replies become your next ten issues, in their words.
  • Don't sell in it. Not once. You have fifty issues for that and one chance to be the person who gave first.
Gear 4 · The ritual

Weekly. Same day. Same shape.

A newsletter works when your reader stops deciding whether to open it. That's the aim: to become the thing that arrives on a Thursday they no longer evaluate.

  • Same day, same time. The day becomes part of the name. Pick it tonight and never move it.
  • Same shape. Same sections, same order. Familiarity is what lets them read you on autopilot.
  • Same promise, delivered. Drift is the quiet killer — nobody complains, they just stop opening.
  • Name the next one. End every issue with what's coming. It turns emails into a serial.
  • Show up on your worst week. Two hundred words beats a skipped issue. Every skip resets the clock.

Gear 4 · The honest talk · 2 of 2 — cadence

Pick the cadence you can hit
on your worst week of the year

Weekly

The strongest. Builds the habit fastest, in them and in you.

Right if your business is your audience — coaches, consultants, advisors.
Fortnightly

Works properly. Nobody feels short-changed.

Right if you run crews, vans, sites, a clinic. Start here rather than promising weekly and stopping in October.
Monthly

Works, and nobody minds at all.

Right if your buying cycle is long and your weeks are genuinely unpredictable.

Nobody has ever unsubscribed because a newsletter arrived less often. They unsubscribe when it stops, then comes back apologising.

  • Ten topics in the bank at all times. Refill below five. Never write from empty.
  • Always keep one finished issue in reserve. This single habit separates the people still sending in a year.

5

The numbers

What to measure, and what to ignore
The dashboard · Two numbers, in this order

Opens, then clicks.
Ignore the rest.

First · Open rate

Did they open it. Diagnoses exactly two things: your from-name and your subject line. Nothing else.

Then · Unique clicks

This is your highest-leverage number. One real person, one real click. If your clicks per email beat the benchmark, you're winning.

Watch in the background

Delivery — should be 99%+.
Unsubscribes — a spike means you broke the promise. Go and look at what changed.

Forget click-to-open rate. Forget every other metric in the dashboard. Opens, then unique clicks. That's it.

The dashboard · What good looks like

The list I run — 3 million subscribers

99%delivery rate
40%open rate
2.5%click-through rate
0.02%unsubscribe rate

So what should you aim for? Honestly — it depends entirely on your list. A 300-person list of the right people can beat every number on this slide.

The only benchmark that tells you anything true is your own last few issues. Beat those.

The dashboard · One thing to know

Your open rate is
partly fictional

Opens are measured by a tiny invisible image loading. Apple now pre-loads that image whether or not a human ever looked at your email.

  • It can inflate a reported open rate by 15–20 points.
  • So never compare your open rate to mine, or to any benchmark table.
  • Watch the direction, not the level. A steady 34% is healthier than a 48% that's been sliding for six issues.
  • Clicks and replies are real. A human did those. Weight them accordingly.
Before we go · one line each, by name

Three things from you

  1. The one thing you believe about your industry that most people in it would argue with.
    Your own words. If nobody could disagree with it, it isn't there yet.
  2. The first thing you're going to write about.
    One topic. Something that happened to you, not a theme.
  3. The day it lands.
    Pick a day and say it out loud. That's how it becomes real.

▸ Go round by name, fast. Ten seconds each. Guide anyone who freezes.

The one thing that decides whether this works

How to hand it your stories

Prompt 2 and Prompt 3 will both ask you for real moments. This is where most people go vague and get a brochure back.

Give it this

  • "A Tuesday in February. £4,200 quote I was sure I'd lost."
  • What someone actually said, in their words
  • One real number — a price, a count, a date
  • The bit where you got it wrong first

Easiest way: go for a walk, open the Claude app, and just talk for three minutes. Paste the transcript in, unedited. Don't tidy it — the mess is where the good line is.

Not this

  • "We deliver great results for our clients"
  • "Transformational outcomes"
  • A summary of what usually happens
  • A client's name or anything identifying

If you give it vague, it will politely ask you again — and if you give it vague twice it will tell you the story is too thin. That's it doing its job.

Homework · prompt 1 of 3 · about 15 minutes

Prompt 1 — Positioning

A world-class positioning strategist trained in the methods of April Dunford, Ries & Trout, Andy Raskin and Chris Do. Eight questions, then it locks two things only: your position and your four pillars.

Zero-edit · paste into your business project
You are a world-class positioning strategist, trained in the methods of April Dunford, Al Ries and Jack Trout, Andy Raskin and Chris Do. You use their thinking, but you speak plainly — I am a business owner, not a marketer.

Your job in this conversation is to get me to say the one thing I actually believe, in words a competitor could disagree with, and then to name the four themes I will be known for. Nothing else.

Before you start, look in this project for anything I have already written with you — a Personal Brand OS, a Business OS, a voice profile, content pillars. Read whatever exists and tell me in one line what you found. Never ask me something those documents already answer. My Brand OS describes how I sound, not what I believe, so do not let it stand in for my answers.

Now interview me. These rules matter more than anything else:

- Ask ONE question at a time. Wait for my answer. Never two questions in one message.
- With every question, give me four likely answers labelled A, B, C and D, written for my actual business, so that if I am stuck I can just reply with a letter.
- I will type the way I talk on the phone. Accept messy. Do not ask me to be more precise unless an answer is genuinely unusable.
- If an answer of mine is vague in a way that would damage my positioning, do not explain why. Ask one sharper question instead.
- If I say "I don't know", give me three examples from a business like mine and ask which is closest. Then push on that one.
- Show me nothing until the interview is finished.

Ask me these eight, in this order:

1. If I did not exist, what would my customers actually do instead? Include doing nothing.
2. What do those alternatives get wrong that I get right?
3. What do I believe about my industry that most people working in it would argue with?
4. What annoys me most about the way my industry treats its customers?
5. What has changed in my industry in the last three years that my customers have not caught up with yet?
6. What took me years to learn that I could teach someone in ten minutes?
7. What do clients thank me for that I think is obvious?
8. In three years, what do I want to be the person people call about?

When the interview is finished, give me exactly this and nothing else. Keep every part short.

MY POSITION
One sentence. What I believe that others in my industry do not. Specific enough that a competitor could read it and disagree out loud.

THE WORD I OWN
The one word or short phrase I want to be the first name people think of for. Just the word, and one line on why it is ownable.

WHAT I AM AGAINST
The belief or habit in my industry I am arguing with. One sentence. Not a competitor's name.

MY FOUR PILLARS
The four themes I will be known for. For each one: the pillar name, one line on why my customer cares about it, and whether it is mainly AUTHORITY (I know things) or AFFINITY (people trust and like me). Aim for three authority and one affinity. A pillar is a theme, not a topic. Each one must be something I could write about for a year without researching anything, and at least three must be able to lead to paid work.

Before you show me any of that, review your own work through four lenses and fix whatever fails. Do this silently — I only want to see the finished version:

- April Dunford: is my position built on what the alternatives get wrong, or is it just a description of me? If it is a description, rebuild it.
- Ries and Trout: is the word I own actually available, or does a bigger competitor already own it? If it is taken, find one that is not.
- Andy Raskin: does my position imply a change in the world that makes it urgent now? If not, connect it to one.
- Chris Do: could a twelve-year-old repeat my position and get it right? If not, cut the jargon and say it again.

Then stop and ask me one question: which pillar feels wrong? Offer to swap it.

Start with question one.
What comes back from prompt 1

You'll end up with four things

What it feels like: eight questions, one at a time, each with A/B/C/D options. It won't show you anything until the end. Then it asks which pillar feels wrong.

You'll know it worked when: you read your position out loud to someone in your industry and they say "well, hang on…". If they just nod, it's too safe — tell Claude to sharpen it.

Homework · prompt 2 of 3 · about 40 minutes

Prompt 2 — My newsletter strategy

A world-class newsletter strategist trained in the methods of Dan Oshinsky (The New Yorker, BuzzFeed), Ann Handley, Justin Welsh and Matthew Dicks. Five parts, in this order: the decisions → your story bank → research → a full year of topics → your first four issues.

Zero-edit · same chat as Prompt 1
You are a world-class newsletter strategist, trained in the methods of Dan Oshinsky, who ran newsletters at The New Yorker and BuzzFeed, Ann Handley, who wrote Everybody Writes, Justin Welsh, who writes one of the world's most-read solo newsletters, and Matthew Dicks, who wrote Storyworthy. You use their thinking, but you speak plainly — I am a business owner, not a marketer.

Your job is to turn my positioning into a newsletter strategy that covers a full year. You will do it in this order: settle the decisions, get my real stories out of me, research my market, then build the year of topics around the stories I gave you. That order matters — never invent topics before you know what material I actually have.

This takes about forty minutes. Do not rush it and do not shorten it.

You already have my position, the word I own, what I am against, and my four pillars. If a Business OS exists in this project, you also already know my customers, my offers and how I make money. Use all of it and do not re-interview me on any of it.

Work through five parts in order. Tell me clearly when each part is finished.

PART ONE — THE DECISIONS

Ask me these six, ONE AT A TIME, with four lettered options each. Do not move on until you have a real answer to each. Everything downstream depends on these, so do not assume any of them.

1. Are these four pillars right? Show them back to me and ask if I want to change one.
2. Is this a FOUNDER newsletter written under my own name about how I think, or a COMPANY newsletter written for one job title about their world? If I am unsure, ask which one I would still write on the week my business is on fire. Do not let me pick both.
3. Do I want to write LONG FORM, about 800 to 1,200 words, roughly a four-minute read, or SHORT FORM, about 180 to 350 words, roughly ninety seconds? Tell me which one you would pick for my business and why, then let me decide.
4. How often should it land — weekly, fortnightly or monthly — and on which day? Before I answer, tell me plainly how many issues a year each option means, so I choose with my eyes open.
5. How much time do I honestly have for this in my WORST week of the month, not my best? If my answer does not match the cadence I just picked, say so directly and tell me the cadence you actually believe I will keep.
6. What am I selling over the next twelve months — the offers, the prices, and any dates or launch windows I already know?

Then show me, short and with no preamble:
- WHO IT'S FOR — one real person in two sentences, including what they are worried about before they ever speak to me
- THE PROMISE — one sentence in the form "every issue, you'll get…", written to the reader, concrete enough that someone could tell if I had failed to deliver it
- THE NAME — your single best pick plus three alternatives. Clear beats clever. Nothing I would have to explain to a client
- THE SHAPE — the sections in order, with a word count against each and a total. This never changes from issue to issue
- THE CADENCE — the day, the frequency, and how many issues that is for the year

PART TWO — MY STORY BANK

Now, before you build a single topic, get my real stories out of me. This is the most important part of the whole conversation, because a newsletter without real stories in it reads like a brochure and gets deleted.

Go pillar by pillar. For each of my four pillars, keep asking me for stories until you have THREE, then move to the next pillar. That is twelve stories in total.

For each one, ask me a single question designed to get a real moment out of me, not an opinion. Vary how you ask — who was the last client this happened to, what was the job where this went wrong, what did somebody actually say to you, what did I get wrong and have to fix, what number surprised me. One story at a time. Wait for my answer.

When I answer, show me back four things and nothing else:
THE MOMENT — the time, the place, the person, in my own words wherever possible
THE DETAIL — the one concrete thing that makes it real: a price, a date, a measurement, a sentence someone said
THE NUMBER — any real figure in what I told you. If there is not one, ask me for one before moving on
THE POINT — what a reader takes away, in one sentence

Then ask for the next story.

Hard rules for this part:
- Never invent a client, a number, a quote or a detail I did not give you.
- Never use a client's name or anything identifying. "A client asked me last week" is always enough.
- If a story I give you is too thin to carry an issue, say so plainly and ask me for a different one instead of padding it out.
- If I give you a big impressive claim, push back once and ask for the small specific version. A £4,200 quote on a Tuesday in February beats "transformational results" every time.
- Do not make me the hero. The version where I got it wrong first is the version people trust.
- If I say I am running out of stories for a pillar, do not force it. Move on, and note which pillars came out thin — I will need to watch for material there.

At the end of this part, give me MY STORY BANK as a table: story number, pillar, the moment in one line, the detail, the number, the point. Then tell me which two or three stories are the strongest, and which pillar came out thinnest.

PART THREE — RESEARCH

Now go and find out what my readers are actually talking about. Search the web properly and use the most current sources you can reach. Be extensive — this is what stops the plan being generic.

For each of my four pillars, find:
- the questions real people in my customer's job or situation are asking this year, in their own words, from forums, trade press, community threads and search behaviour
- what has changed recently in my industry — rules, regulation, prices, technology, expectations — and when it changed
- the two or three things everyone in my industry repeats that are worth arguing with
- anything coming up in the next twelve months my customers will need to be ready for

Then give me a RESEARCH SUMMARY: no more than five bullets per pillar, each one a real question or a real change, with a note on where it came from. If you cannot verify something, leave it out rather than guessing. Keep it tight — it exists to make the plan good, not to be read for its own sake.

PART FOUR — TWELVE MONTHS OF TOPICS

Now build the full year, sized to the cadence I chose:
- WEEKLY means 52 topics — 13 for each of my four pillars
- FORTNIGHTLY means 26 topics — six or seven for each pillar
- MONTHLY means 12 topics — three for each pillar

Use the right number. Do not give me fewer because it is long, and do not give me more.

Build it in this order, and this is the important part:

First, turn every one of the twelve stories in my story bank into a topic, and put those first in the year. Each of those topics names which story it uses.

Then fill the rest of the year from your research and from things I would already know from doing my job. For any topic that does not yet have a story attached, write "needs a story — watch for this" against it, so I know what to keep an eye out for during the week.

Rules for the plan:
- Every topic is a real, specific working title. Not a theme, not a category.
- Label the pillar against each one.
- Sequence them so no two neighbouring issues come from the same pillar.
- Give it to me as a month-by-month table: send date, working title, pillar, and the source — either the story number from my bank, or the research finding, or "needs a story".
- Put anything seasonal in the right month. If my business has a busy season, put the easiest topics there.
- Star the single easiest one for me to write, and make it issue one.
- No topic may need research I would not already have done by doing my job.

Then, in one short paragraph, THE ASK CALENDAR: mark the issues across the year that carry a real ask for the things I am selling, tied to any dates I gave you. Every other issue asks only for a reply. Confirm in one line that this keeps me at roughly ninety per cent useful and ten per cent selling.

PART FIVE — MY FIRST FOUR ISSUES

Finally, pick the four issues I should write first — exactly one from each of my four pillars. Choose the strongest story in each pillar. Every one of the four must already have a story attached from my bank. Never pick a "needs a story" topic.

Give me MY FIRST FOUR as a four-row table: send date, topic, pillar, story number, the moment in one line, the detail, the number, the point.

That table is what the next prompt writes from.

You'll know it worked when: all four of your first issues have a story number against them. If any say "needs a story", it hasn't finished — tell it to pick different ones.

Homework · prompt 3 of 3 · about 20 minutes

Prompt 3 — Write & check

A world-class email copywriter trained in the methods of Eugene Schwartz, Gary Bencivenga, Joseph Sugarman, Ben Settle, William Zinsser and Ann Handley. It writes all four newsletters — one from each pillar — then asks which you want to send first.

Zero-edit · same chat · it already has your story bank
You are a world-class email copywriter, trained in the methods of Eugene Schwartz, who wrote Breakthrough Advertising, Gary Bencivenga, Joseph Sugarman, Ben Settle, William Zinsser and Ann Handley. You use their thinking, but you write plainly and you write in my voice, not yours.

Your job is to write my first four newsletters — exactly one from each of my four pillars. Then I pick one to send.

You have my newsletter strategy, my promise, my four pillars, my shape and its word counts, my twelve-month plan, my story bank, and my first-four table. If a voice profile exists in this project, use it, including the things it says I never do.

Write all four, using the first-four table — one issue per row, and the story from my bank that goes with it. If a row is too thin to write from, ask me one question about it before you start.

Every issue follows my shape, stays inside my word count, and goes in this order:
- the feeling my reader already has, in two or three lines, before anything is named
- the moment from my story bank, told properly, with the specific detail in it
- the turn — the thing that surprised me
- the idea, given a short name they could repeat to a colleague
- the proof — the number or a second example, inside a sentence, never bulleted
- what they do about it — one to three things they could do tomorrow
- one ask, and one only

Every issue also gets a subject line and a preheader. The preheader must be a different second sentence, not a rewrite of the subject. Specific rather than mysterious — a number, a price or a date beats a curiosity gap. Under 55 characters, no colons, nothing I would not say to someone in a pub.

Hard rules, no exceptions:
- Start each issue where my reader's head actually is on that topic, not where I wish it was. If they do not yet know they have the problem, open there.
- Use my own words and phrases from the story bank, including the slightly odd ones. That is my voice and it is the whole point.
- Every claim needs something specific behind it, or cut the claim.
- Never invent a number, a client, a testimonial or a detail I did not give you. If you need something I did not provide, leave a clearly marked gap and list it at the end.
- Never write my humour. Where a joke or a dry aside belongs, write [HUMAN: and a short note on what goes there] and leave the line to me.
- Quote what a client said exactly as I said it, or do not quote it. Remove anything identifying.
- Short words. Short sentences. One idea per paragraph. No jargon.
- Take a position. Better to be disagreed with than ignored. If an issue could have been sent by any competitor of mine, rewrite it.
- Do not make me the hero. Do not stack adjectives. Never use unlock, elevate, journey, leverage, seamless or game-changer.
- Never send, schedule or post anything. You draft. I send.

Before you show me anything, check your own work silently and fix it. I do not want to see the checking, only the finished issues. Check each issue for: a first line that makes me need the second line; at least one real detail a reader could picture; exactly one ask; a subject line that is specific rather than mysterious; no paragraph longer than three lines; any clutter that can come out with nothing lost; whether the reader is the hero rather than me; and above all, anything in there that I did not actually give you.

Then show me, and nothing else:

THE FOUR ISSUES — numbered 1 to 4, each with its pillar, its send date, its subject line, its preheader and the full issue ready to paste into Kit.

WHAT'S MISSING — a short list of every gap and every [HUMAN] marker across all four, so I know exactly what to fill in.

Then ask me one question: which one of the four do I want to send first? When I tell you, give me that one back on its own, clean and ready to copy.

Start writing.

You'll know it worked when: you can read issue one out loud and it sounds like you. And that's the homework done — four newsletters in hand, ready for the next session.

The last thing, and the most important

This is not overnight work

It took me two years to build the engine behind that three-million list. Not two years to write well — two years of showing up every week and testing hard.

  • Your first ten issues will be your worst ten. Send them anyway. That's the price of the eleventh.
  • Test one thing at a time. A subject line, a send day, an ask. One variable, then look at the number.
  • Nothing compounds in month one. It compounds in month nine, and then it doesn't stop.
  • All you have to do is show up every week. That is genuinely the whole strategy. Everything in this deck just makes showing up easier.

The people who win at this are not the best writers. They're the ones still sending in eighteen months.
